newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin resurfaces, G7 leaders rally behind him.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin resurfaces, G7 leaders rally behind him.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who missed a late-night gala concert at the Group of Seven summit, resurfaced on Sunday looking well and other leaders rallied behind him.

"It's good to see you in good shape. When I see you I'm always in a good mood," French President Jacques Chirac said at the start of talks with Yeltsin before the summit's final session. Chirac later said Yeltsin looked "excellent."
The 66-year-old Russian leader spoke clearly and coherently to reporters as he left his hotel.

But he again walked slowly and stiffly when he joined his fellow leaders for the last round of talks, and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had to help him turn on his translation device after seeing him fumble with it.
Yeltsin, who has a history of mysterious disappearing acts, had at least two heart attacks last year and his absence from the concert on Saturday prompted speculation about his health.

Stephanie Denning, spokeswoman for the Denver Health Medical Center, said an ambulance was sent to Yeltsin's hotel as a precaution on Saturday night after the president left a dinner with G7 leaders early.
"He was not feeling well after dinner. He went directly to his hotel. We did send an ambulance to his hotel but it was never used," she said. "He was taken care of by his personal physican."

Yeltsin had seemed to be enjoying himself at Saturday's dinner before leaving. Spotting a large stuffed rattlesnake at the restaurant, he took his wife Naina's hand, made her touch it in fun and forced a squeal out of her.
Russian reform chief Anatoly Chubais said the president had simply been "a little bit tired".

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said: "It is obvious that after the hard work of the two days, plus the altitude and the heat, the president required some extra rest. In fact the other leaders could hardly fight off sleep."
U.S. President Bill Clinton rallied behind Yeltsin as he summed up the results of three-day summit. "I thought he did an extraordinary job," he told a news conference.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said Yeltsin had looked fitter than at a summit with NATO leaders in Paris last month.
"We did not even realise something had happened. I thought he was in better form than in Paris," Prodi told reporters.
Kohl, Yeltsin's closest ally in Europe, also gave him his support by saying Russia could at some stage host a summit of the eight nations which gathered in Denver.
Chirac made clear that he approved of Yeltsin's decision to give the concert a miss.
"You were right yesterday night," he told Yeltsin. "All the others sat down and fell asleep, especially (Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro) Hashimoto -- a very deep sleep."

The Denver summit, also attended by the leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, was Yeltsin's first long excursion from Russia since he had heart surgery last November.
Denver is more than 5,000 feet (1,550 metres) high in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains and visitors are warned about the debilitating effects of altitude.
Yeltsin failed to appear for a meeting with Japan's foreign minister in 1992 and left Irish officials standing on the tarmac dring a stopover at Shannon airport in September 1994.
